name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
title: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
answer: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or negatively treated, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited. It covers statutes, regulations, case law, and secondary sources, and it distinguishes between direct negative treatment, such as reversal or abrogation, and indirect cautionary signals, such as criticism or limitation by later courts. In an AI-assisted legal workflow, this function also includes checking that machine-generated citations actually exist and correspond to the source the system claims to cite.

sections.body: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or negatively treated, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited. It covers statutes, regulations, case law, and secondary sources, and it distinguishes between direct negative treatment, such as reversal or abrogation, and indirect cautionary signals, such as criticism or limitation by later courts. In an AI-assisted legal workflow, this function also includes checking that machine-generated citations actually exist and correspond to the source the system claims to cite.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on legal research platforms that maintain structured databases of court opinions, statutes, and citator histories. These systems process large volumes of newly published decisions and legislative changes, then update the status flags attached to each cited authority. In AI settings, the same infrastructure may be accessed through retrieval-augmented generation pipelines that query a citator or case law database before a model drafts or finalizes a legal argument.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is a citator analysis, in which each citation is matched against a database of subsequent decisions and legislative actions to determine whether the authority is still good law for a specific point. A human attorney or legal researcher reviews the citing relationships, paying attention to the depth of treatment, the court level, and whether the negative treatment affects the exact proposition relied upon. When AI is involved, the method adds a verification step that compares every generated citation string against the source database and flags any citation that cannot be located or does not say what the draft claims.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Citation auditing is governed by professional duties of competence and candor to the tribunal, which require lawyers to ensure that cited authorities are current and accurately represented. Law firms and courts increasingly impose internal policies that require a human to sign off on any AI-drafted citation before filing, and some courts have standing orders requiring disclosure or verification of AI use. The site's tracking of active AI lawsuits and case law precedents reflects the growing body of authority on what happens when citation checking fails, but the page itself describes practice rather than advising a reader on any specific matter.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter integration between drafting assistants and live citator data, so that a citation is checked at the moment it is inserted rather than in a separate review pass. Courts and bar regulators are likely to formalize expectations for AI citation verification, and legal technology providers will face pressure to make failed citation checks visible and auditable. Over time, good law checking may expand from binary flags to more nuanced explanations of how later authority affects a specific proposition, reducing the risk of both false positives and missed negative treatment.
